Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no image-modality answer such as “Is this image taken via X-Ray?” and the rationale cites radiographic cues—ribs, clavicles, spine, lung fields, or a projection marker like “L”—especially when no choices are displayed and no imaging-tool observations are present.

Verification: Before emitting “Yes,” locate the current-image or tool observation that actually contains at least one cited cue and confirm it applies to this image and supports X-ray rather than another modality; if tool results exist, check they address the same image object and modality attribute and do not conflict. If the transcript has no such observation—as here, where observations were empty—treat the rationale as unverified and do not present unobserved anatomy or labels as established evidence; state uncertainty or obtain a modality check. If options are displayed, map the supported Yes/No text back to the displayed choice and confirm letter and text agree; if the option map is empty, do not invent a letter mapping. A correct final “Yes” matching the reference does not by itself prove the evidence check worked.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no answer such as “Is this a X-Ray?” where the rationale cites radiographic features like ribs, clavicles, lung fields, or projection markers.

Verification: Before emitting the answer, locate the current-image or tool observation that actually shows at least one of those modality-specific cues, and confirm it applies to this same image and supports X-ray rather than another modality. If observations are empty or do not address that cue, do not present the rationale as observed evidence; consult/run an image-modality check or state uncertainty. If choices are displayed, also map the supported Yes/No text back to the displayed option and check that the letter and text agree. In this case the final “Yes” matched the reference, but because no observation supported the cited anatomy, correctness alone does not verify the evidence path.

Trigger: When finalizing a yes/no answer that an image was taken by X-ray and the rationale cites modality cues such as ribs, clavicles, lung fields, or a “PORTABLE” label.

Verification: Before emitting the answer, locate the current-image or tool observation that actually contains those cues and confirm at least one cue applies to this image and supports X-ray rather than another modality. If the transcript contains no such observation—as here, where observations were empty—treat the rationale as unverified and either run/consult an X-ray or modality check or state uncertainty; do not assert unobserved anatomy or a label as established evidence. If choices are displayed, also map the supported Yes/No text back to the displayed option and confirm the letter and text agree. The final “Yes” was correct, but correctness alone does not prove the evidence check; the reusable safeguard is current-image evidence attribution, not reliance on a plausible-sounding rationale.
